Anchor 1: Values: TEAM framing (no community present). Efficiency, optimization and cost reduction dominate; removing the human is treated as a gain: "AV can anticipate the shortage of food. No communication from human" (CLUSTER: Communication, [Idea]). A relational minority pushes back: "How might we ensure there is a human element/touch with AVs used as a social service for those they serve, delivery" (CLUSTER: Logistics, [HMW]).
Anchor 2: Capabilities and Constraints: Constraints the team names FOR the community: time poverty, information gaps, being homebound, aging volunteers, missing rural infrastructure. "How might we design a moving spaces to solve neighbors service access issues (time constraint, information gap)" (CLUSTER: Community Resource Connection, [HMW]). Capability-as-asset framing is largely absent; the community is framed as a problem to solve, not a set of existing capacities.
Anchor 3: Meanings and Practices: Mobility framed almost entirely as logistics: moving food, supplies and labor between banks, pantries and doors. "Community AV that all pantries have access to for pantry to pantry transportation (volunteers, food, supplies)" (CLUSTER: Food Supply Demand, [Idea]). A competing meaning surfaces in a few stickies: "Using AV's to pick up people instead of food" (CLUSTER: Logistics, [Idea]).
Anchor 4: Misalignment: This transcript is itself an artifact of the misalignment: efficiency logic is the design team's own first instinct, not an outside vendor's. Face verification and access codes vs low-barrier help: "Should have some sort of face verification to ensure food is handed to the right person" (CLUSTER: Privacy, [Idea]). Loneliness reframed as a machine feature: "Senior citizens are lonely, become friends with AV" (CLUSTER: Logistics, [Idea]). Value at stake: relational trust.
Anchor 5: Provocation: YES, the whole session is a speculative AV brainstorm (internal team). Ideas: mobile pantries and common spaces that park and wait for neighbors; AVs as connective infrastructure linking farmers, banks, pantries and families; AVs for people not food (rides to medical appointments, homebound neighbors, aging volunteers); refrigerated AV storage for pantries. "How might AV help home bound neighbors come to the pantry" (CLUSTER: Home Bound Neighbors, [HMW]). Concerns attached: client data privacy, keeping a human in delivery, not losing the pantry as a social hub. No sticky names who would be excluded.

Anchor 1: Values: STAKEHOLDERS and planners (no clients present). Social service framed as relational, not transactional, and named as something AV design must be deliberate about: "Social service meaning relational engagement not transactional" (SECTION: What would AV address, cluster header). Transit-equity value: serve where people need to go. End-user burden proposed as the success measure against financial ROI: "new metrics that measure the weights of burden" (cluster: ROI).
Anchor 2: Capabilities and Constraints: Constraints: transportation is a top client barrier but chronically underfunded and never funded as a primary service ("It is often bundled as a need with grants for other areas rather than being funded as a primary service", cluster: Funding & decision criteria); fixed-route transit cannot serve the singular or the first/last mile; pantry hours collide with work hours; federal food-program rules generate the friction; homebound people are left out of the ideation itself. Capability framing is thin; nearest is the MPO Serve committee that includes transit riders.
Anchor 3: Meanings and Practices: For homebound people the delivery is the human contact: "Delivery person might be the only point of human contact the home bound people might have" (cluster: Home Bound). The existing system already moves people to food and food to people through overlapping programs run with heavy coordination cost. Debated: should the AV move food, move people, or move people with food. Routes are drawn by housing density and infrastructure counts; food deserts named as a factor "but not yet" used.
Anchor 4: Misalignment: Planning done without the community: "Neighbor have ideas imposed on them. Their needs are not accommodated" (cluster: People centered, Input/decision making). Value: community participation. Transit optimized for the most people by design does not serve the singular or homebound (equitable access). Funders bundle and underfund transportation (equitable access). Financial ROI is the wrong yardstick for a public-good service. Automaker interest openly named as the driver: "Biggest ROI of AV as a social service is the adoption rate of AV" vs "Serving Automakers interest in building infrastructure" (board annotation). Value: MaSS vs product-adoption logic.
Anchor 5: Provocation: YES, board framing questions are "Barriers for AVs adoption", "How would AV works in terms of service?", "What would AV Address". Reactions: skepticism it is a general solution ("AV cannot be designed for everyone. It's not the next big solution", cluster: Personalized services); regional and institutional reluctance to adopt at all; strongest positive use case is small AVs as micro-transit shuttles for the first and last mile between transit lines and pantries; AV as capacity multiplier for the network. Binding condition: it must be intentionally relational and not one-size-fits-all. A cited pilot stat ("G2G Program: 85% success with AV") has no source in the transcript.

Anchor 1: Values: Mutual care as unquestioned duty: "Nothing. I don't ask questions. Look at you saying nothing. I don't get it. I don't ask questions." (00:20:56, Speaker 5). Dignity, pride and stigma around asking, sometimes overcoming one's own past judgment ("I ain't going to no pantry... But that was me... I'm the person who need it now", 00:22:35, Speaker 8). Being known earns exceptions. Faith and the pantry as the last safety net: "The pantry is all we got to rely on." (00:17:58, Speaker 1). The ideal meal is people and completeness, not food: "I want freedom from being broke." (00:14:09, Speaker 1).
Anchor 2: Capabilities and Constraints: Capabilities: sustained informal care distribution ("Monday through Thursday I'm at her house", 00:20:31, Speaker 8, on a 93 year old neighbor), lifelong neighborhood knowledge, entrepreneurial skills and credentials, a car that turns one person into a distribution node. Constraints: benefit cliffs ("my dad was $74 over... so you don't get nothing", 00:41:07), hours cut 40 to 20, no license ("I've never had a license", 00:47:10), bus stops far from destinations, food desert with predatory pricing, pantry stocks food only not household or hygiene goods, a 2020 record blocking rehire.
Anchor 3: Meanings and Practices: Mobility is caregiving: "you're going to different places trying to just get enough to feed two or three households" (00:20:13, Speaker 8). One client wakes at 6 a.m. to stand in line, then redistributes to the homebound. Pickup is from inside cars; in winter the line is a line of vehicles and the carless are exposed. Clients also move information, briefing each other on benefit changes, a proposed shelter, a data center. The researcher names the care work as infrastructure: "carrying each other. That's very precious, kind of using the terms infrastructure." (00:54:18, Speaker 2).
Anchor 4: Misalignment: In-person self-collection rule vs the homebound the community is feeding: "She can't get out and get this. But then you can't take it to her because the person has to be here to get the benefits." (00:19:42, Speaker 8); rule rationale is fraud prevention. Zip-code eligibility gates better-stocked pantries. Saturday-morning hours collide with work. Food-only stock misses household and hygiene needs. Hiring systems surface old records. Institutions dropping "community" from their names: "you took the community out" (00:57:03, Speaker 2). Automation arriving in low-wage work without consultation (White Castle kiosks).
Anchor 5: Provocation: YES, the researcher raises driverless vehicles twice. Cautious yes, framed through personal mobility gaps: "I would take a car. You know why?... I don't know how to drive. I've never had a license. If a car could drive me... I could put the address in and I'll just sit there and go, la, listen to my music, dance, and the car just be rolling on where I'm going." (00:47:10, Speaker 7). Use cases named: reaching destinations the bus does not, not standing in the winter cold. Backdrop of fear that automation is already taking jobs ("Oh, yeah, it's horrible"). Bus vouchers volunteered as the low-tech version: "bus vouchers would be good for people, too." (00:48:32, Speaker 8).

Anchor 1: Values: Mutual aid extended to homeless neighbors at the door: "it ain't just for me and my family it's other people in our neighborhood that know there's homeless... i'll come up to the door and you got something i can eat." (00:46:25, Speaker 3). Intergenerational family living as a deliberate care model ("we're like the old school where you got all the family living", 00:26:11). Being listened to is itself a service: "Sometimes you just need someone to listen to you." (00:42:32, Speaker 3). Several "ideal meal" plates are memorials to a lost spouse.
Anchor 2: Capabilities and Constraints: Capabilities: deep knowledge of the resource landscape (Community Compass, 211, produce days), self-taught cooking adapted for a diabetic household, shared-household meal logistics five days a week, peer help ("I work in real estate on the side. I can try and help you navigate that", 00:09:10, Speaker 7). Constraints: a broken-down car threatening a job orientation, cannot afford glasses because of property taxes, a home misclassified as commercial and never given the homestead deduction in eight years, unresolved medication interactions, transportation named as why neighbors cannot reach the pantry.
Anchor 3: Meanings and Practices: The pantry visit is one node in a redistribution circuit: surplus cooked into daily meals handed out at the door. Mobility inside the household: "Everybody goes to somebody else's different days." (00:35:09, Speaker 7). For this group the pressing trip is to work and to a job orientation, not only the pantry. Information mobility is constant (which pantry stopped stocking meat, which store is cheaper). Outreach should be face to face: "not everybody has the phone. sometimes just putting a couple people out handing out [flyers]" (00:45:16, Speaker 3).
Anchor 4: Misalignment: A nearby pantry replaced first-come-first-served with a card-shuffler lottery: "you can be the first ones in line and not get out. Until six o'clock at night." (00:22:13, Speaker 7). Value: flexibility for variable need and respect for time. No food choice, leaving diabetic clients with starch. A pantry narrowed its stock to snacks. Resource navigation gated behind a smartphone. A mandatory monthly class where the program failed to tell enrolled clients it had started. Property-tax system defaulted a widow's home to commercial, doubling her bill. Transit the intended riders cannot afford: "what's the sense in having a public transportation if you still can't afford the public transportation" (00:49:50, Speaker 7).
Anchor 5: Provocation: YES, the facilitator raises AVs directly. Qualified yes with an immediate misuse concern rooted in neighborhood knowledge: "I think it would, but it would have to be on issues... they could be using it for drugs" (00:48:34, Speaker 3). Concrete design condition offered by participants: "limit the destinations to like pantries and grocery store" (00:49:07 to 00:49:19, Speakers 3 and 7). Who it would help: older people who cannot drive and cannot afford the bus on a fixed income. Bus passes again volunteered as the immediate fix.

Anchor 1: Values: Single-informant interview with a community weaver / advocate. Help as a universal obligation and a self-perpetuating cycle: "help is universal. To extend your hand" (13:28). The church pantry is trusted because it is read as compassionate and non-judgmental. Shame and pride are the defining emotional texture across cultures: "welfare, food, you're in the pantry, you're dirty. It's almost like the mental ill still, stigma." (55:51). The pantry as a social and dignity space, not only food. Independence voiced as the client goal, sometimes as never wanting to come back.
Anchor 2: Capabilities and Constraints: Capabilities: the weaver is himself dense infrastructure (20 years, 3 pantries, recruits interpreters from among clients); multilingual refugee clients ("they speak six, seven... languages. We speak one", 11:50); word-of-mouth networks ("the original internet right there", 01:13:45); a client surplus-swap; resourcefulness in use. Constraints: transportation is named as the single biggest obstacle (no bus stop near the pantry, no sidewalks, walking with a box and children); language barrier at computer intake; no phone, wifi, or literacy for a digital job application; childcare cost exceeds the wage; benefit cliffs; demand tripled.
Anchor 3: Meanings and Practices: The pantry trip is routine and a source of stability: "It's almost like, yeah, coming to a job almost." (01:00:58). Multi-pantry circuits, two or three pantries a week. Walking with a stroller as a cart, cutting through a Dollar General lot because there is no safe route. The weaver runs a personal delivery route for homebound neighbors and a Christmas box operation that scaled to about twenty drivers. Information moves by mouth and by weekly sign-up tables at the pantry.
Anchor 4: Misalignment: Shift from a choice or "shopping" model to a pre-packed box under volume pressure: "Now we just put it in the box and move on. Because... the volume got so much from 100 to 350, 400, we couldn't just keep letting them stay in there." (15:03). Visit frequency rationed from weekly to twice a month against continuous need. Card, number and ID intake. Adding a bus stop stalled behind an IndyGo feasibility study while people walk with boxes in the cold. A data-collection rule stopped the pantry recording nationality, hampering interpreter planning. The new building designed as a drive-through for flow. FSSA renamed "family and social resources". Hiring moved online, closing the walk-in route.
Anchor 5: Provocation: NO. No AV, automation, or future-mobility prompt was asked. Adjacent, not AV: the transportation-solution conversation is entirely low-tech; the weaver is lobbying IndyGo for a bus stop and names gas cards and bus passes as the resources to build out: "Resource for like bus passes and stuff like that. We're gonna start trying to do that too. Gas cards" (54:12).
